title: Women rabbis
hook: Reform ordains a woman in 1972, Reconstructionist in 1974, Conservative in 1985; Orthodox communities debate women's roles

segments.voice: Yesterday, bat mitzvah, and your line: a girl at a lectern. Did you mark a girl's milestone? Today, the question that girl's generation left for the next ones. Day one thousand forty-one.

Five sisters walk up to Moses, in front of the priest, the leaders and the whole congregation. Their names are Mahlah, Noa, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, the daughters of Zelophehad. Their father has died with no sons, and with no son to inherit, his name and his share of the land will be lost to the family. They ask: why should our father's name be done away? Give us a possession. Moses doesn't answer on his own. He brings their case before God. And the answer comes back: "The daughters of Zelophehad speak right." A new law of inheritance follows. Hold on to those sisters. Today's story is about women standing up, in front of everyone, and asking the tradition a question.
screen: `FIVE SISTERS BEFORE MOSES.` → `THEY ASK A QUESTION OF THE LAW.` → `THEY SPEAK RIGHT.`

segments.voice: At the end of the same chapter, Moses hands leadership to Joshua. "And he laid his hands upon him, and gave him a charge." That laying on of hands is called semikhah, and it's the word Jews still use for rabbinic ordination. For a long time, only men received it. Then the movements of modern Judaism each faced the sisters' kind of question, and answered in their own time and their own way. Reform Judaism ordained a woman rabbi in 1972. The Reconstructionist movement followed in 1974. The Conservative movement, after a long debate over Jewish law, in 1985. Each of those decisions came with arguments from the sources, and people on more than one side. In Orthodox communities the question is still open, and argued with real seriousness. Some Orthodox institutions now train women in Jewish law and give them roles with new titles, teaching, answering questions, serving congregations. Other Orthodox authorities hold that the rabbinate belongs to men, and that women's leadership should take other forms. Both sides argue from the same Talmud, the same codes, the same respect for the law. So today isn't a story with a finish line. It's a picture of how Jewish law moves: someone asks, the community argues, and sometimes the answer changes and sometimes it doesn't, and either way the question stays open to the next person who asks. That's today's line. The debates continue.
screen: `SEMIKHAH: HE LAID HIS HANDS.` · `REFORM, RECONSTRUCTIONIST, CONSERVATIVE.` · `ORTHODOX VOICES ON BOTH SIDES.` · `THE QUESTION STAYS OPEN.` · then, large: `THE DEBATES CONTINUE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: respect paths unlike yours. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind a community whose practice differs from yours, or from what you'd choose: a synagogue, a church, a mosque, a family down the street. Don't argue with it in your head. Instead, try to name what it is protecting, what it loves, what it's afraid of losing. If it helps, think of the five sisters and of Moses: a question asked in public, and an answer that took time. Let your breath carry the difference without needing to settle it. The bell holds the time.
Women rabbis. Ordained in the Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative movements, and still debated, seriously and from the sources, in Orthodox communities. Today's word.
Your line: the debates continue. Today, learn one practice of a community unlike yours, and ask what it is protecting. Day one thousand forty-one.

howItsDone: Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative seminaries ordain women as rabbis and cantors; in Orthodox communities some institutions train women for teaching and advisory roles under new titles, while other Orthodox authorities hold that the rabbinate is for men.

notes: Claims rule: the three dates come from the index hook and are attributed to it ('the index gives the dates'). The first women ordained (Sally Priesand, Sandy Eisenberg Sasso, Amy Eilberg) are not named; consider adding names if wanted.

Orthodox debate: described without ranking; 'some Orthodox institutions' (e.g., Yeshivat Maharat) and 'other Orthodox authorities' (e.g., the positions of the Orthodox Union and Rabbinical Council of America) are unnamed. Please confirm the framing is fair to both sides.
'Semikhah' as the term for ordination, from laying on of hands (Numbers 27:23): please confirm.
Numbers 27:7 and 27:23: please confirm the JPS 1917 wording of the quoted portions.

Editor pass: hook now follows Numbers 27:4 (the sisters ask why their father's name should be done away) instead of claiming a stated law; removed the spoken 'the index gives the dates' and 'since the dates the index gives'; cut the mind-reading 'neither side thinks the other doesn't care'; 'the argument stays inside the family' and the carry's 'say its best reason back' were too close to day 1035 (arguing at one table; saying the other view back fairly), so the close and the carry action now point to learning what another community's practice protects.
Audit: 'The law is changed' replaced with 'A new law of inheritance follows' (Numbers 27:8–11), since rabbinic readings differ on whether the law was changed or newly revealed.
